claims.text: NSAIDs: start 24–48 h before menses and continue until 1–2 days after menses begin; no NSAID is clearly better than another, and COX-2 inhibitors are no more effective
claims.quote: NSAIDs are usually started 24 to 48 hours before and continued until 1 or 2 days after menses begin. There is little evidence for superiority of any individual NSAID for pain relief or safety and no evidence that COX-2 specific inhibitors are more effective (1).

claims.text: Estrogen/progestin contraceptive: estrogen prevents ovulation and progestin thins the endometrium → less arachidonic acid for prostaglandin synthesis → ↓ menstrual blood flow and contractions
claims.quote: Estrogen prevents ovulation and progestin thins the endometrial lining leading to less arachidonic acid to be used for prostaglandin synthesis, thus reducing both blood flow and contractions during menses (3).

claims.text: Progestin options (also for secondary dysmenorrhea due to endometriosis): progestin-only pills, oral dienogest, levonorgestrel IUD, etonogestrel implant, depot medroxyprogesterone acetate
claims.quote: Other hormone therapy may also be effective for primary dysmenorrhea or as treatment of secondary dysmenorrhea due to endometriosis. Progestin therapy options include oral progestins (eg, progestin-only oral contraceptives, oral dienogest), levonorgestrel intrauterine device, etonogestrel implant, or depot medroxyprogesterone acetate.

claims.text: GnRH agonists decrease dysmenorrhea but may cause low-estrogen side effects; danazol is an option but rarely used (androgenic adverse effects)
claims.quote: Gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonists (GNRH) were effective at decreasing dysmenorrhea but may have low estrogen side effects (4). Danazol is also an option, but is rarely used due to androgenic adverse effects.
